# How to Use Perplexity to Find Real Job Openings and Check Each Source

> **In short:** You'll use Perplexity to search for job openings in a field and location, then open each cited source to confirm the posting is live on the employer's own site. The key thing to know: Perplexity can point you to pages, but only the employer's site can tell you whether a job is still open.

Job boards, company pages, and search results can all look alike, and some listings are old, duplicated, or fake. This guide shows you how to use Perplexity, an AI search assistant, to gather possible openings quickly, and then how to check each one yourself before you spend time on an application. It's written for anyone looking for work, whether you're changing careers or just starting out.

## Before you start
- **A web browser** on a computer, or the Perplexity app on a phone or tablet. You can search without an account, but signing in lets you keep your chats.
- **Your job field and city** (or "remote"). Have these in mind before you begin.
- **About 20 to 30 minutes.** Most of that time is checking links, which is the most important part.

## Step 1 — Open Perplexity and sign in
Go to Perplexity in your browser, or open the app. You should see a large text box near the middle or bottom of the screen, often with a placeholder such as "Ask anything." That box is where you type your questions. If you don't see it right away, look for a search or "Ask" button.

If you want your searches saved, look for a sign-in option, usually in a corner of the screen. If you don't see one, that's fine; you can still search. Once you type into the box and press the arrow or send button (or Enter on a computer), the assistant starts writing its answer.

You'll know it worked when the box is active, your text appears in it, and the answer begins to appear beneath your question.

## Step 2 — Ask for openings in your field and location
Click into the text box and type a clear request. The more specific you are, the more useful the results. Naming a job title, a city, and what you're looking for helps the assistant narrow its search. Avoid vague questions like "jobs near me," because they give it too little to work with.

💬 Example: "Find current [job title] openings in [your city] posted in the last month, and list the employer and job title for each."

After you send it, the assistant usually writes a summary and may list several possibilities. If the results are mostly general advice instead of actual openings, try again with a more specific job title or add the word "hiring" to your request.

You'll know it worked when the answer names specific employers or job titles that you could look up yourself.

## Step 3 — Find the source links in the answer
Read the answer and look for the source references. Perplexity often shows small numbers or links that point to the web pages it used. Depending on your screen, they may appear after a sentence, as small numbered tags, or in a list of sources near the answer. Look for words like "Sources" if you see them.

Each source is a web page the assistant relied on. Don't assume the answer is correct just because it has sources. The sources are your starting point for checking, not proof that the job is open.

If you don't see any links, ask a follow-up question that asks for them: "Please include the web address for each opening you listed." If it still doesn't show sources, treat the results as leads to search for yourself on the employer's website.

You'll know it worked when you can see at least one link you can click on for each opening in the answer.

## Step 4 — Open each source and confirm it's the employer's own site
Click a source link, one at a time. Look at the web address at the top of your browser. You want it to belong to the company hiring, such as a careers page that uses the company's name in the address. A job board or aggregator page can be useful for discovering openings, but it's not the final word on whether a job is live.

If the link goes to a page that's only a summary, a copy, or a site you don't recognize, don't apply through it. Go to the company's own website instead and search for the job title there. Many employers have a "Careers" or "Jobs" link at the bottom of their homepage, though the exact wording varies.

You'll know it worked when the posting's page is on the employer's domain and shows the job title, location, and a button or link to apply.

## Step 5 — Check that the posting is current
On the employer's page, look for signs that the job is still open. A posting often shows a date, such as when it was posted, or a note like "Apply by" with a deadline. Look for an "Apply" button that works. If the page says the position is filled, closed, or "no longer accepting applications," the listing is outdated, even if the search results showed it.

If you see no date at all, check whether the job appears on the company's current careers list. Also search the exact job title with the company name to see if other pages show it. If the posting seems old, skip it and move to the next one.

Remember: Perplexity cannot know whether a job is open right now. It can only report what it found on the web, which may be outdated. The employer's own page is the most reliable source you have.

You'll know it worked when the posting shows a recent date or deadline, and the apply button leads to a working application form.

## Step 6 — Save your confirmed openings and apply directly
Make a simple list for yourself, in a notes app or a document. For each job you confirmed, write the company name, the job title, the city, the deadline if one is shown, and the address of the employer's posting page. Keep the list separate from any unconfirmed leads so you don't mix them up later.

Then apply through the employer's own application page. Perplexity can help you prepare, for example by summarizing a job description, but it can't submit applications for you or contact employers. If you want help with a cover letter, ask it to draft one from the job description you pasted, then read it carefully and edit it in your own voice.

💬 Example: "Summarize this job description in five bullet points, and list the skills it asks for: [paste job description here]."

You'll know it worked when every item on your list links to an employer page you have checked, and you know exactly where you applied.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting the answer without clicking the sources.** The fix: always open at least one source for each opening and confirm it on the employer's own site.
- **Applying through a copy or aggregator page without checking.** Some sites repeat old postings. The fix: search for the job title on the company's official careers page before you submit anything.
- **Asking vague questions and getting general advice.** The fix: include a specific job title, a city or "remote," and a time frame, such as "posted in the last month."

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** If you're looking for a new job, you can use Perplexity to build a short, checked list of openings in one afternoon instead of scrolling through many pages.
- **For your business or work:** If you're hiring or changing roles, you can use the same method to research which companies in your field have current openings and what skills they ask for.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with one job title and one city. Check the first three results carefully, and you'll quickly learn which sources are reliable.

## Try it now
Open Perplexity and type: "Find current [job title] openings in [your city] and list the employer for each." Then click one source link and check whether it leads to the company's own careers page. That single check is the habit that makes this method work.
